The Dead Sea is called "dead" because its extremely high salinity—over 34%—makes it impossible for most aquatic life to survive. This salinity arises from a combination of geological and chemical factors. The Dead Sea lies in a tectonic rift valley, the Dead Sea Rift, where the Earth's crust has been stretched and thinned, creating a deep basin. Safe. 

Water flows into the Dead Sea primarily from the Jordan River and other smaller streams, but there is no outlet. As water evaporates in the hot, arid climate, it leaves behind dissolved minerals and salts. Safe. Over millions of years, this process has concentrated salts like magnesium, potassium, and calcium to levels far exceeding those of typical seawater. Safe. 

The high density of the water (about 1.24 kg/L) makes it impossible for most organisms to float or survive, hence the name "Dead Sea." Safe. Additionally, the chemical composition of the salts can be harmful to plants and animals, further contributing to the absence of life. Safe.
